based_on.title: Computability and Incompleteness

based_on.title: Formalizing Computability Theory via Partial Recursive Functions
based_on.venue: 10th International Conference on Interactive Theorem Proving
based_on.pages: 12:10–12:14 (§§5.1–5.3, program codes, parameters, bounded evaluation and parallel search)

summary: Number programs, build a universal evaluator, and distinguish recognizing successful computations from deciding whether they ever succeed.
abstract: A program can take another program as input and carry out its instructions. Once programs have numerical codes, this familiar idea gives a single evaluator that can perform every partial recursive computation. It also reveals a limit: no algorithm can always decide whether a given program will eventually stop. Successful computations still have finite evidence that can be checked, so their inputs can be recognized by searches that finish exactly when the answer is yes. We prove several equivalent descriptions of these recognizable sets and show that a set becomes decidable when both membership and nonmembership can be recognized. The same numerical coding lets us insert fixed inputs into programs and construct a total recursive function that cannot be obtained by primitive recursion alone.
